scenes.visual_summary: Slide summarizing Fermat's Last Theorem with the central equation 'a^n + b^n = c^n', a horizontal timeline spanning more than 350 years from c. 1637 to 2026, and a bottom callout box titled 'What made it hard'.
ocr_details: A one-line claim that stood unproven for more than 350 years
has no solutions in positive whole numbers when n is greater than 2
When n = 2 there are endless solutions, such as 3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2
c. 1637: Fermat writes the claim in the margin of a book
1980s: Frey, Serre and Ribet tie it to a deep conjecture
1993: Wiles announces a proof, and a gap is found
1995: Wiles and Taylor publish the proof: 129 pages in all
2026: First complete computer-checked proof, in Lean
The statement is simple, but the proof needed a link between two distant areas of mathematics, elliptic curves and modular forms.

spoken_segments.text: So, Fermat's Last Theorem is one of the more kind of famous claims in mathematics. It stood unproven for around 350 years, and it's actually a very simple statement, just a to the n plus b to the n equals c to the n has no solution for any positive whole numbers greater than two.

Now, this deceptively simple kind of statement has proven to be quite difficult to actually prove. In the mid-90s, Sir Andrew Wiles did prove it. He put out a proof, and it took him 7 years of work, it was extremely painstaking.

And since that time, a major effort and interest in mathematics has been formalizing that proof, where basically computationally checking every step. So proofs are kind of long chains of logic and you actually can computationally check proofs using different systems, what I'll talk about for example using Lean.

scenes.alignment_note: The speaker points toward the slide equation 'a^n + b^n = c^n', the 'More than 350 years' timeline (referencing 1993/1995 Wiles proof and the 2026 Lean entry), while explaining the history and formalization goal.

scenes.visual_summary: Screenshot of a YouTube video titled 'Beauty is Suffering [Part 1 - The mathematician]' showing Sir Andrew Wiles working at a wooden desk piled high with handwritten mathematical manuscripts, with a 'Source' link beneath.

spoken_segments.text: So this is just kind of a visual kind of explaining—there's a very interesting video showing the effort that he went through; it is an extremely painstaking process to establish this proof.

scenes.alignment_note: The speaker gestures toward the YouTube video screenshot of Andrew Wiles surrounded by stacks of paper to illustrate how painstaking manual proof work is.

scenes.visual_summary: Slide quoting an article excerpt titled 'Formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem' with pink/red highlighter emphasis on the first three sentences explaining proof assistants like Lean and a second paragraph noting the 86-page blueprint.
ocr_details: One way to check a proof's correctness is to ask a computer to do it. Proof assistants like Lean verify the logic of a proof algorithmically, demonstrating its correctness beyond a doubt. The difficult part for humans is rewriting the proof so Lean can understand it. While a proof written for human readers will skip many obvious steps, Lean needs to see every step, no matter how trivial. Human proofs also build on centuries of published work, while a formalization starts from the tiny fraction of math that's been formalized already.
For FLT, the formalization process was expected to take years. Just the blueprint the mathematical community has been using to describe the initial phase of the project runs to 86 pages.

spoken_segments.text: And in September we published that we used Claude to formalize it. This is like the first very important result that we kind of shared along these lines. And we used Lean to do it, so Lean allows you to computationally verify every step in a proof. Now doing this though is extremely painstaking.

scenes.alignment_note: The highlighted sentences on screen directly correspond to the speaker's explanation of using Lean to verify every single logical step computationally.

spoken_segments.text: So, this is just giving you a sense for the harness. It looks kind of complicated but it's actually pretty simple. Each of the thousand agents has its own sandbox with restricted network access. Most of this is directed on safety and security. So, we have a thousand agents. Each have their own sandbox. They can connect to two different things, Git and a SQL database, that's it. Those are the core primitives that we give this team.

And we have real-time monitoring looking at every tool call for things like escapes. We also have offline monitoring looking at runs of all the agents every 10 minutes. This is kind of the setup. Thousand agent team, very simple primitives, just Git and a database.

The prompting is pretty simple. It establishes one lead agent, 999 helper agents. It gives them awareness of Git and the database and the problem statement, that's really it. We want to see if this team could then do this formalization.

A table where the lead can announce things, assign roles to workers, everyone can—agents can post notes, a subtask table, a table that indicates whether or not things are landed. So the lead just creates these tables to orchestrate this team.

spoken_segments.text: This, from one of our runs, this is one of the notes that the agents left, basically saying total freeze of the origin effective now, magnificent work all 999 of you.

So, basically, what is really interesting about this is we were able to show this formalization, which was expected to take many, many years. Back in September, we showed initially we could do it with like a dozen agents with a lot of scaffolding—this Prove2Me harness and a lot of poking and support from a researcher. This new result is showing we provide a lot of structure in terms of safety and monitoring, but the agent team was able to accomplish this task with very simple primitives without a domain-specific harness in this particular case. And agents are getting increasingly good at orchestrating themselves and knowing how to coordinate using these simple primitives for very challenging long-horizon tasks. That's really the key kind of observation which is very interesting from this work.

spoken_segments.text: Now I want to shift gears and talk about memory, which is entirely different when I talk about in terms of multi-agent, but it's highlighting another area where we're seeing Claude gain significant capability. So previously we talked kind of about Claude's ability to orchestrate large teams to solve very long horizon problems. Memory is a different capability. It's showing that Claude is increasingly capable to organize its context to help solve long horizon problems.

scenes.alignment_note: The 'Memory' section slide appears right as the speaker states 'Now I want to shift gears and talk about memory'.

scenes.visual_summary: Quote slide displaying '"Life can only be understood backward, but it must be lived forward."' attributed to Søren Kierkegaard.
ocr_details: "Life can only be understood backward, but it must be lived forward."

spoken_segments.text: So, I published a blog on this fairly recently. And this is actually the lead line of the blog, and I think this actually encapsulates the idea of the blog and one of the central ideas around memory, I think is very interesting. And this is from the philosopher Kierkegaard, so life can only be understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards.

There is a fundamental paradox of agent memory because agents write to memory typically as they go about a task. They encounter something weird or interesting, they write to memory. But memory needs to be a coherent map of an agent's knowledge that agents can look back on and reflect on. So when they're writing to memory, they're writing kind of myopically, they're looking greedily within a session saying, oh, this seems important for this task at hand. But memory needs to be something that's globally coherent and not redundant.

So this is like a very tricky paradox of memory and frankly we as humans have the same kind of challenge. We go about our day, we write short-term memories—believe that the hippocampus kind of is the place that's orchestrated. At night, it's believed that the hippocampus replays to the neocortex, which is where long-term knowledge is stored. So it's believed that actually this dreaming process for humans helps consolidate the fragments or like the most important aspects of our daily experience into long-term knowledge. So there's this decomposition between daily memory and kind of long-term knowledge. And we found agents can benefit from the same decomposition. That's really the key point of the post.

scenes.alignment_note: The speaker reads the Kierkegaard quote on screen and uses it to frame the paradox between live, myopic memory writing and retrospective consolidation ('dreaming').

scenes.screen_title: CL-Bench database task & Accumulated reward over questions
scenes.visual_summary: Two-panel benchmark slide. Left panel ('CL-Bench database task') is a grouped bar chart comparing 'With memory store' (solid bars) vs 'Stateless baseline' (hatched bars) across Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5, Opus 4.7, Sonnet 5, and Sonnet 4.6. Right panel ('Accumulated reward over questions') shows running mean reward across questions 1 to 30+ for each model with and without memory.
ocr_details: Question number (running mean of all questions so far)

spoken_segments.text: Now here's some results kind of telling the story. So this is actually an open-source continuous learning benchmark called CL-Bench. And this is showing that different models, as you go from like Sonnet up to like Opus 5, get increasingly good at using memory. Now this task is a very simple setup. It asks Claude to solve 40 questions about a database. In between each question, it's a fresh session and Claude can write to notes like a memory directory between each session.

So what happens is the dark bars are showing when you give Claude the memory store and then the hatched is like without memory, okay? Now what's interesting is with Sonnet 4.6, giving Sonnet memory, you can see in the dark blue, that's very little benefit. Can't really use memory. And we looked into the results and we found Sonnet doesn't reliably know when to write to memory and also doesn't really naturally read from memory, okay?

It's also worth noting that these experiments are done with no specific memory prompting. It just tells the agent the directory is available, use memory if you want, that's really it. So Sonnet 4.6 doesn't natively use memory effectively. Sonnet 5 does indeed better, Opus and so on. And so basically, the models get better and better with the same simple instruction in using memory. And really the key idea here is that what happens is, with stronger models, they know intrinsically when to write to memory and they kind of know intrinsically when to read from memory to retrieve information. Their memories are also better—they're like highly verified statements or predictions about kind of the state of the database or what may happen next, versus earlier models tend to write lower quality memories.

scenes.alignment_note: The speaker points to the dark blue vs hatched bars on the far right ('Sonnet 4.6' 0.364 vs 0.351) to show minimal memory benefit, then gestures left toward 'Sonnet 5' and 'Opus' bars where the gap widens dramatically.

spoken_segments.text: And I'll show you a very fun example of this from a different game. This is from Pokémon. So this is showing you Claude 3.7's memory directory from Pokémon versus Fable 5. Here's the key point: the size of each box indicates the number of memory files in each of these directories, okay? So when we have Claude play Pokémon, we give Claude a memory directory just like I did in that prior benchmark, right? Claude can write whatever it wants to a directory while it plays the game.

What's really interesting is Sonnet 3.7 we see it writes a huge amount to memory. And when we look at the memories, it's indiscriminate. It's basically writing down all sorts of experience; it creates this huge unwieldy just disgusting memory directory of things that are not really relevant or strategic for gameplay, and it proceeds much worse in the game than Fable 5.

Fable 5's memory directory is much tighter. It's really strategic insights, tactical knowledge, things you can't just get from game state very easily. So what we see is better models have much better instincts for salience and like what to write to memory and you can see this reflected in the size of the memory directories—it's much tighter, it's much more strategic in gameplay. Indeed, Fable 5 gets much further than Sonnet 3.7.

So it gives another intuition around the fact that Claude is much better at writing to memory, knowing kind of what to write and salience and what's salient, and also kind of using and reading from memory. So models are getting more and more kind of effective at knowing salience, knowing what to write, and also reading.

Now, both of these represent what I would consider, in my initial framing, of like writing to memory during experience. So basically, in both of these tasks, we let Claude write to memory while it plays this game, we let Claude write to memory while it does the CL benchmark. But as I mentioned, there's also the dreaming side of memory. This is allowing Claude to reflect over memories, to fix things, and I'll show some interesting examples of that.

spoken_segments.text: This is kind of a framing of dreaming. And so you can think about memory in terms of—there are transcripts. Transcripts you can think about as kind of the foundation of memory. So imagine a memory system could very simply be just transcript search. Claude writes a transcript as it goes about a task, future sessions can read from the transcript. Of course transcripts are large, it's very unwieldy. We talk a lot about in the blog post the fact that transcripts often contain a very small amount of information that is actually salient and matters.

So, we also allow Claude to do things like writing memory notes, also what I just talked about—as it goes it can write notes to memory. But dreaming lets you do more. Dreaming lets you reflect over transcripts and these written notes, and represent them, build memory representations like wikis as an example, actually promote certain memories to injected context and load it preemptively into every future session. So dreaming is this mechanism where you can kind of process existing transcripts or existing memory notes and build new things from them including representations, injected context, and more.

spoken_segments.text: So some fun examples of this: this is from Pokémon gameplay. Dreaming is an effective way to correct mistakes in memory, so as I talked about, when Claude's going about a task, it can write incorrect notes to memory. Just, it makes a mistake. This happened in this particular game: Claude incorrectly wrote the location of a particular landmark in the game. Now what happened is, with this incorrectly written memory, Claude got trapped in a loop, where basically it would mislocalize itself at this particular point in the game, fall down this trap door, and it would basically send it back to the prior level.

That's like the high level intuition, the details aren't that interesting or important. The key idea is a poison memory was injected and it's stuck there. Dreaming can rescue that; that's really the intuition on why dreaming is extremely powerful for reflecting over memories and correcting them.

spoken_segments.text: So this is showing some trajectory of the game, where orange is memory and dreaming. Up is good, so basically up represents game progress, and down represents kind of game regression. And what's interesting is raw memory, basically without dreaming, we can see crashes out—an incorrect memory is planted and Claude continues to basically regress or fall in the game when it hits that particular point. With dreaming, it rescues that mistake, Claude proceeds to the next level. That's really the key observation and this is a very general principle: that Claude can use dreaming to correct mistakes in memory that are otherwise stuck there. It's a very important way you can kind of correct from errors.

spoken_segments.text: Now, this is another fun example of building representations in memory. So, there's been a lot of interest in wikis as kind of general ways that Claude can organize knowledge. This is a really fun example from—we acquired a company, Stainless, back in May. And we had access to the company corpus, all its documents and Slack messages and so forth, and we anonymized things and we built kind of a dataset from it which allowed us to test dreaming.

So what we did was we created kind of an eval setup: 25 questions about the company that can only be answered from this corpus. We allow Claude to build a wiki from this information to help it answer questions. What you see is we compare a raw search tool, that's just like some kind of semantic search over this documentation. We compare that as a baseline, which does reasonably well—you can see it's like 53% just for search.

We also test letting Claude build a wiki over this knowledge. You can see as you add more and more dreaming tokens, the wiki gets better and better and better, allowing Claude to answer questions. So Claude natively can kind of build up over time a representation of this corpus of knowledge through a wiki. And as you add more dreaming compute, that wiki gets more and more useful. We think this is a really nice mental model to think about how agents can kind of build knowledge over time.

We also find that adding the wiki and the search tool together actually bumps further beyond just raw search. So this is kind of another intuition that basically Claude can also build representations like wikis in its kind of memory, in order to help it kind of solve problems.

spoken_segments.text: And a final example, this is from a different benchmark, but this is showing two different wikis that Claude built. So this is prior to dreaming and after dreaming. What we saw is when Claude was building wikis in this particular case, there were some gaps. And for example, this initial wiki had a bunch of placeholders for pages that didn't exist. This can happen when Claude is kind of building different memory representations, and without dreaming compute, there may not be opportunities to rescue or fix those errors.

What we saw is when we ran dreaming, dreaming can look over Claude's existing representation like for example a wiki and can fill in mistakes. So in this case, it fills in a lot of missing gaps, it creates an index. And so again, dreaming is a way that Claude can reflect and kind of apply compute across its memory to improve it by correcting mistakes like I talked about, by filling in gaps in its knowledge like we see here, or for example by creating new representations like wikis.
